newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank likely to keep rates steady - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank likely to keep rates steady - analysts.

text.p: The Bundesbank is likely to hold key German interest rates unchanged for at least two more weeks, feeling no pressure to loosen its monetary reins even after a set of soft economic data, economists said on Tuesday.

In a Reuters poll on the prospects for an interest rate change at this week's bi-weekly council meeting of the German central bank, 10 economists were unanimous in forecasting the key discount, Lombard and repo rates would be kept steady.
Arguing that even weak October industrial production output did not change the overall picture, economists said there were no compelling arguments for the Bundesbank to adjust interest rates.

"In the current economic environment there is no need for further monetary impulses, rather monetary policy is already clearly expansive due to the weaker mark and stronger dollar," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
Hammering home that point, the Bundesbank restated comments made earlier by its president Hans Tietmeyer that rates would remain steady in the short term.

Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber, speaking shortly after October industrial output figures showed a 1.8 percent drop on the month, said: "I would draw your attention to recent comments by Mr Tietmeyer in the Spiegel magazine, when he observed - I see no short term reason for another interest rate change".

Economists said the Bundesbank had acted early to quell any potential revival of interest rate cut speculation but added this may not have been necessary as the markets showed no signs of expecting a rate cut.
"Market prices are not showing revived interest rate speculation," said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.

In addition to arguing there was no immediate need to cut rates, economists said there was no no room for a cut if the Bundesbank intended to stick to its main policy target for M3 money supply. M3 remains above the four to seven percent growth rate.
"The Bundesbank will keep its Lombard, discount and repo rates unchanged as money supply growth remains above the target zone," Ralf Kugelstadt, economist at UBS in Frankfurt, said
Several economists said the Bundesbank is becoming slightly more flexible in allowing monetary policy to be guided by money supply growth, seen as an indicator of future inflation rates.
But the Bundesbank, facing no need to cut interest rates, could afford to be appear quite rigid in sticking to its targets -- making a rate reduction look unlikely.

Economists were equally convinced the main money market rate, the repo, kept at a fixed three percent rate since late August, would not be lowered. They did not expect the Bundesbank to revert back to its favoured method of offering variable rate tenders.

As the Bundesbank generally reverts to a fixed rate tender to smooth out any end-year spikes in money market rates, any thought of shifting back to a variable rate pact would not be considered until next year, several economists said.

There is a small chance, however, the Bundesbank may announce it will exempt the repo business from minimum reserve holdings, which would help shore up the German repo market and boost the nation's position as a financial centre.
Bundesbank council members have said the topic has been discussed at several meetings but that certain technical issues still needed to be worked out.
A decision is expected on the issue before the end of the year, and some economists said the council may prefer to announce the deal at the year's final meeting on December 19.
